title: TMEM55B Maintains Lysosomal Homeostasis and Promotes ER–Lysosome Calcium Signaling

paragraphs.en: Membrane contact sites (MCSs) between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and late endosomes/lysosomes (LE/Ly) are established through specific tethering complexes rather than random membrane encounters. ORP1L and VAP were among the first proteins identified as ER–LE/Ly tethering factors, and subsequent studies have shown that numerous lipid transfer and trafficking proteins—including members of the ORP, STARD and LAM families, as well as NPC1, Protrudin, and PDZD8—function at these sites [1, 2, 3]. ER–LE/Ly contacts increase during endosomal maturation, a process closely associated with both lysosomal acidification and Ca2+ signaling. Cholesterol and Ca2+ therefore serve as key mediators of communication between these organelles at ER–LE/Ly MCSs [4].

Cells obtain cholesterol through two major pathways: de novo synthesis and endocytic uptake of lipoproteins (LPs) [5, 6, 7]. In the brain, cholesterol is produced predominantly by glial cells and delivered to neurons via HDL‐like LPs. Following receptor‐mediated endocytosis, cholesteryl esters (CEs) are hydrolyzed by lysosomal acid lipases to generate free cholesterol, which is subsequently distributed to the ER and other organelles for cellular functions [4, 7, 8, 9]. In parallel, CEs stored in lipid droplets (LDs) can be degraded through lysosome‐dependent lipolysis, allowing lysosomal lipases to mobilize stored lipids [10, 11, 12, 13]. Efficient lysosomal maturation and acidification are therefore essential for cholesterol metabolism derived from both LPs and LDs.

PDZD8 is an ER membrane protein originally identified as a Protrudin‐interacting protein and functions at ER–LE/Ly MCSs [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. PDZD8 belongs to the TULIP superfamily and contains a synaptotagmin‐like mitochondrial lipid‐binding protein (SMP) domain that mediates lipid transfer [16, 21, 22]. Together with Protrudin and VAP proteins, PDZD8 contributes to cholesterol trafficking at ER–LE/Ly MCSs [3]. We previously demonstrated that PDZD8 deficiency impairs lipolysis and causes CE accumulation in the brain, indicating an important role for PDZD8 in cholesterol metabolism [23, 24, 25]. Consistent with these findings, abnormal CE accumulation has also been reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients and AD mouse models [26, 27, 28]. Moreover, neurons carrying the APOE4 allele, the strongest genetic risk factor for AD, exhibit lysosomal dysfunction accompanied by CE accumulation and lipofuscin formation [29, 30]. Despite the established role of PDZD8 in cholesterol metabolism, the mechanisms by which it regulates lysosomal function remain poorly understood.

In addition to cholesterol metabolism, increasing attention has focused on lysosomal Ca2+ signaling. During endosomal maturation, luminal acidification is accompanied by progressive accumulation of Ca2+ within endolysosomal compartments, making lysosomes an important intracellular Ca2+ store [31, 32, 33, 34]. Luminal Ca2+ promotes endosomal maturation through intraluminal vesicle fusion, whereas Ca2+ release from lysosomes contributes to diverse signaling pathways. In particular, calcium‐induced calcium release (CICR), whereby lysosomal Ca2+ release triggers secondary Ca2+ release from ER‐localized IP3 receptors and ryanodine receptors, has emerged as an important mechanism for intracellular Ca2+ signaling [35, 36, 37, 38, 39]. Endolysosomal acidification also regulates the activity of lysosomal Ca2+ channels such as two‐pore channel 2 (TPC2) and TRPML1. Although Ca2+ signaling at ER–LE/Ly MCSs has been implicated in multiple cellular processes [34, 40], the molecular mechanisms coordinating lysosomal acidification, Ca2+ dynamics and lipid metabolism remain incompletely understood.

TMEM55B is a lysosomal membrane protein with multiple reported functions. Originally identified as a phosphatidylinositol phosphatase that converts PtdIns(4,5)P2 to PtdIns(5)P [41, 42], TMEM55B was subsequently shown to associate with the v‐ATPase and Ragulator complexes, thereby contributing to lysosomal signaling and mTORC1 activation [43]. Consistent with its importance, TMEM55B knockout mice are embryonic lethal [43]. Because v‐ATPase is essential for endolysosomal acidification, disruption of this pathway results in lysosomal dysfunction and storage disorders [44, 45, 46]. TMEM55B has also been implicated in dynein‐dependent retrograde lysosomal transport, oxidative stress responses, and regulation of LDL receptor expression [47, 48, 49, 50]. However, whether TMEM55B contributes to lipid metabolism through regulation of lysosomal acidification and Ca2+ signaling remains unknown.

In the present study, we identified TMEM55B as a lysosomal protein that binds the Protrudin–PDZD8 complex and demonstrated that TMEM55B contributes to the maintenance of lysosomal function as well as Ca2+ dynamics in lysosomes and the ER. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which TMEM55B cooperates with the Protrudin–PDZD8 complex to regulate lysosomal function at ER–lysosome MCSs.

sections.title: Protrudin–PDZD8 Complex Interacts With the Lysosomal Protein TMEM55B

paragraphs.en: The Protrudin–PDZD8 complex promotes endosomal maturation at ER–LE/Ly MCSs, but how these ER proteins contribute to the regulation of lysosomal function has remained unclear. To identify lysosomal proteins interacting with PDZD8, we established a Neuro2A cell line stably expressing 3 × FLAG‐tagged PDZD8. The PDZD8 complex was isolated by anti‐FLAG immunoprecipitation, separated by SDS‐PAGE, digested with trypsin, and analyzed by LC–MS/MS. In parallel, the same analysis was performed using cells transfected with empty vector to exclude nonspecific binding. Proteins reproducibly detected across three independent experiments were extracted, and semiquantitative analysis based on identification frequency (IF) [51] identified 196 proteins with IF > 0.01. Among those, 13 endosome‐localized proteins were selected using GO Term and UniProt subcellular localization annotations (Figure 1A). Protrudin was identified as the protein that interacted most strongly with PDZD8. This finding is consistent with a previous report identifying PDZD8 as the protein that interacted most strongly with Protrudin, suggesting that the two proteins form a robust complex. Among the lysosomal proteins, TMEM55B and its binding partners, the v‐ATPase subunit Atp6v0d1 and Lamtor1, were included (Figure 1A) [43]. Notably, Lamtor1 and TMEM55B are lysosome‐localized proteins associated with cholesterol metabolism, suggesting a potential role in endosomal maturation through cholesterol transfer. Since TMEM55B regulates the v‐ATPase complex, we focused on TMEM55B as a candidate upstream regulator of PDZD8‐dependent lysosomal function. However, because PDZD8 and Protrudin form a robust complex, we next examined which of the two proteins TMEM55B binds more directly. By immunoprecipitation and immunoblot analysis, interactions between PDZD8 and TMEM55B (Figure 1B) and between Protrudin and TMEM55B (Figure 1C) were confirmed. We next examined the intracellular distribution of PDZD8, Protrudin, and TMEM55B and found that PDZD8 and Protrudin were localized predominantly to the ER, whereas TMEM55B was localized predominantly to lysosomes (Figure 1D). We further examined whether pairwise co‐expression of these three proteins altered their intracellular distribution. Co‐expression of PDZD8 and TMEM55B did not alter the localization of either protein (Figure 1E), whereas co‐expression of PDZD8 and Protrudin (Figure 1F) or of Protrudin and TMEM55B (Figure 1G) altered their respective localizations and induced prominent aggregate formation, suggesting a strong interaction. These results suggest that TMEM55B binds more directly to Protrudin than to PDZD8. Together, these findings demonstrate that TMEM55B interacts with the Protrudin–PDZD8 complex.

sections.title: TMEM55B Is Not Essential for ER–LE/Ly Tethering

paragraphs.en: Because PDZD8 functions as a tether at ER–LE/Ly MCSs, we examined whether its binding partner TMEM55B also contributes to this process. TMEM55B expression was suppressed in HeLa cells using siRNA (siTMEM55B), resulting in a marked reduction of both RNA and protein levels compared with control cells (siControl) (Figure 2A,B). To assess ER–LE/Ly contacts, we employed a split‐GFP system in which GFP fluorescence is reconstituted only when ER and lysosomal membranes are closely apposed [16, 52]. Cells were co‐transfected with ERj1‐GFP (1–10) (ER‐localized fragment) and LAMP1‐GFP (11) (lysosomal fragment), together with mCherry to normalize expression levels. The GFP/mCherry fluorescence ratio per cell, reflecting ER–LE/Ly MCS formation, was quantified (Figure 2C). No significant difference in GFP/mCherry ratio was observed between siTMEM55B and siControl cells (Figure 2D). These results demonstrate that, unlike PDZD8, TMEM55B is not required for tethering of ER–LE/Ly MCSs.

TMEM55B interacts with the v‐ATPase complex, suggesting its involvement in the regulation of this complex. We therefore hypothesized that TMEM55B contributes to lysosomal acidification and activity via v‐ATPase. To test this, HeLa cells transfected with siControl or siTMEM55B were stained with LysoTracker (Figure 3A) or LysoSensor (Figure 3C), both of which increase in fluorescence intensity as lysosomal pH decreases. In both assays, siTMEM55B cells showed significantly reduced fluorescence intensity compared with controls, suggesting that lysosomal acidification may be impaired (Figure 3B,D). However, because the fluorescence of these acidotropic lysosomal probes does not necessarily reflect pH alone, it cannot be concluded definitively that TMEM55B depletion impairs lysosomal acidification. We further analyzed lysosome number, morphology, and size using the LysoTracker fluorescence signal, and found no abnormalities in lysosome number per cell (Figure 3E,F) or morphology (Figure 3E,G) in siTMEM55B cells, whereas lysosome size was reduced (Figure 3E,H). However, because the LysoTracker fluorescence signal was weak in siTMEM55B cells, we cannot exclude the possibility that lysosomes merely appeared smaller as a result. Nonetheless, the reduction in acidotropic lysosomal probe fluorescence upon TMEM55B depletion demonstrates that TMEM55B contributes to the maintenance of lysosomal function.

sections.title: TMEM55B Promotes Ca2+ Release From the ER

paragraphs.en: Intracellular Ca2+ elevation promotes lysosome fusion with other organelles [44], suggesting that lipolysis mediated by the PDZD8–TMEM55B complex could involve Ca2+ signaling at ER–LE/Ly MCSs. Since the ER is the major intracellular Ca2+ store, we investigated whether TMEM55B regulates Ca2+ release or uptake from the ER. HeLa cells were transfected with the ER‐targeted Ca2+ indicator G‐CEPIA1er [53], which binds ER luminal Ca2+ and emits GFP fluorescence, and colocalization with the ER marker KDEL was confirmed by confocal microscopy (Figure 4A,B). To assess ER Ca2+ dynamics, siControl or siTMEM55B cells were stimulated with ATP to induce transient ER Ca2+ release, followed by Ca2+ reuptake to the ER. In siTMEM55B cells, ATP‐induced ER Ca2+ responses were markedly attenuated in siTMEM55B cells compared with controls (Figure 4C). Quantitative analysis demonstrated that TMEM55B depletion reduced the peak ER Ca2+ response (Figure 4D), decreased the initial rate of ATP‐induced ER Ca2+ release (Figure 4E), delayed the time required to reach peak release (Figure 4F), and slowed the subsequent recovery phase (Figure 4G). These findings indicate that TMEM55B facilitates ATP‐stimulated transient Ca2+ release from the ER.

sections.title: TMEM55B Promotes Ca2+ Release From Lysosomes

paragraphs.en: We next investigated whether TMEM55B regulates Ca2+ release from lysosomes and how this affects ER Ca2+ dynamics. Lysosomal Ca2+ release and uptake were monitored using Ly‐GG, which binds cytosolic Ca2+ at the lysosomal membrane and emits GFP fluorescence [54] (Figure 5A). Co‐expression of Ly‐GG with the lysosomal marker LAMP1 confirmed colocalization (Figure 5B). ATP stimulation of siControl HeLa cells induced transient Ca2+ release from lysosomes. ATP‐induced lysosomal Ca2+ responses were markedly attenuated in siTMEM55B cells compared with controls (Figure 5C). Quantitative analysis revealed reduced rates of lysosomal Ca2+ release and reuptake (Figure 5D,E). As a control, we examined mitochondrial Ca2+ using CEPIA3mt [53], which binds mitochondrial matrix Ca2+, together with the mitochondrial marker Su9‐RFP [55] (Figure 5F), which confirmed colocalization (Figure 5G). ATP stimulation induced transient mitochondrial Ca2+ increases as well as decreases, which were not significantly different between siControl and siTMEM55B cells (Figure 5H–J). These results indicate that TMEM55B specifically regulates lysosomal Ca2+ dynamics without affecting mitochondrial Ca2+.

sections.title: TMEM55B Acts to Maintain Lysosomal Function

paragraphs.en: Introduction of siRNA against human TMEM55B revealed abnormalities in the lysosomal luminal state and in ER–lysosome calcium signaling upon TMEM55B depletion. To exclude potential off‐target effects of the siRNA, we further performed rescue experiments by introducing mouse TMEM55B cDNA. For LysoTracker analysis, EGFP‐tagged mouse TMEM55B was introduced, and cells in which EGFP fluorescence was confirmed were analyzed (Figure 6A). The reduction in LysoTracker signal caused by TMEM55B depletion tended to be restored by expression of EGFP‐TMEM55B (Figure 6A,B). For calcium signaling analysis, HA‐tagged mouse TMEM55B was introduced, and we confirmed by immunoblotting that it was expressed at a level comparable to that of endogenous human TMEM55B (Figure 6C). In the G‐CEPIA1er analysis, which detects ER luminal Ca2+, the G‐CEPIA1er response that was reduced by TMEM55B depletion was restored to a level comparable to that of control cells (Figure 6D,E). Similarly, in the Ly‐GG analysis, which detects Ca2+ in the vicinity of lysosomes, the Ly‐GG response that was reduced by TMEM55B depletion was restored to a level comparable to that of control cells (Figure 6F–H). Together, these results demonstrate that TMEM55B acts to maintain the lysosomal luminal state and ER–lysosome calcium signaling, thereby playing an important role in the maintenance of lysosomal function.

Endosomal maturation via ER–LE/Ly MCSs is essential for lysosomal integrity, and cholesterol and calcium transport across these contact sites is thought to play an important role in this process. Disruption of ER–LE/Ly MCSs has also been implicated in numerous neurodegenerative diseases. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying endosomal maturation have remained incompletely understood. The Protrudin–PDZD8 complex is a central component of ER–LE/Ly MCSs that promotes endosomal maturation, but how this ER complex promotes endosomal maturation had been unclear. In the present study, we identified TMEM55B as a binding partner of the Protrudin–PDZD8 complex and showed that TMEM55B contributes to the maintenance of lysosomal homeostasis and to the regulation of ER–lysosome calcium dynamics.

However, whether the Protrudin–PDZD8 complex and TMEM55B function in the same pathway in lysosomal regulation remains unclear and warrants further investigation. It also remains unclear whether TMEM55B‐mediated regulation of lysosomal function is by v‐ATPase, and this issue requires further study. In addition, although cholesterol and calcium transport at ER–LE/Ly MCSs has been implicated in endosomal maturation, the present study did not address the involvement of cholesterol, which likewise remains to be examined. Furthermore, we used acidotropic lysosomal probes to assess the lysosomal luminal state in this study; because these probes can be influenced by factors such as membrane potential, membrane integrity, and probe uptake, verification with more precise pH probes will be needed to clarify the contribution of TMEM55B to the reduction of lysosomal pH.

Loss of TMEM55B impaired lysosomal Ca2+ release and uptake, as well as ATP‐stimulated Ca2+ release from the ER, while mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics remained unaffected. In our system, lysosomal Ca2+ release peaked within 180 s after ATP stimulation (Figure 5C), whereas ER Ca2+ release peaked later (Figure 4C), consistent with calcium‐induced calcium release (CICR) from the ER triggered by lysosomal Ca2+ release. However, because the Ca2+ reporter responses in the ER lumen and in the vicinity of lysosomes were measured in separate experiments in this study, we could not determine the directionality or causal relationship of the Ca2+ signals between the two organelles, and this issue remains to be clarified in future studies. Nonetheless, TMEM55B may act to maintain lysosomal luminal homeostasis, thereby preserving the normal activity of lysosomal Ca2+ channels, maintaining lysosomal Ca2+ signaling, and contributing to CICR at ER–lysosome MCSs.

sections.title: Cell Culture, Transfection, and Retrovirus Infection

paragraphs.en: HeLa cells (CCL‐2, purchased from ATCC, US) were cultured under a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 at 37°C in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (Invitrogen Life Technologies) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Invitrogen Life Technologies). The culture medium for Plat‐E cells was also supplemented with blasticidin (10 μg/mL). Cells were transfected with the use of XtremeGene9 reagents (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) according to the manufacturer's protocol. For retroviral infection, Plat‐E cells were transiently transfected with pMX‐puro–based vectors and then cultured for 48 h. The retroviruses in the resulting culture supernatants were used to infect Neuro2A cells, and the cells were then subjected to selection with puromycin (1 μg/mL).

sections.title: Identification and Categorization of PDZD8‐Associated Proteins

paragraphs.en: Neuro2A cells infected with a retrovirus encoding FLAG–tagged mouse PDZD8 or with the corresponding empty virus were solubilized in a lysis buffer (40 mM HEPES‐NaOH [pH 7.5], 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.5% Triton X‐100, 1 mM Na3VO4, 25 mM NaF, aprotinin [10 μg/mL], leupeptin [10 μg/mL], 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride) to prepare whole‐cell extracts. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation at 20400 × g for 15 min at 4°C. The clarified supernatants were subjected to affinity purification with anti‐FLAG (M2)–agarose affinity gel (Sigma‐Aldrich), and then proteins eluted with FLAG peptide (Sigma‐Aldrich) was separated by SDS‐PAGE and stained with silver. The stained gels were sliced into pieces, and the abundant proteins therein were subjected to in‐gel digestion with trypsin. The resulting peptides were dried, dissolved in a mixture of 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid and 2% acetonitrile, and then applied to a nanoflow LC system (Advanced UHPLC; Michrom BioResources, Auburn, CA, USA) equipped with an L‐column (C18, 0.15 by 50 mm, particle size of 3 μm; CERI, Tokyo, Japan). LC–MS/MS analysis was performed with an Orbitrap Velos Pro instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All MS/MS spectra were compared with protein sequences in the International Protein Index (IPI, European Bioinformatics Institute) mouse version 3.44 with the use of the MASCOT algorithm. Assigned high‐scoring peptide sequences were considered for correct identification. Identified peptides from 3 independent experiments were integrated and regrouped by IPI accession number. Proteins detected in ≥ 2 of 3 independent experiments from FLAG‐PDZD8–expressing cells, but absent from control cells, were considered PDZD8‐associated. Semi‐quantitative abundance was estimated from identification frequency (IF; number of identified peptides per protein normalized to the number of theoretically detectable tryptic peptides). Functional categorization of PDZD8associated proteins was categorized with use of the UniProtKB database (https://www.uniprot.org) based on Gene Ontology (GO) annotations. The proteins listed in Figure 1A are annotated as endosome‐related (GO: 0005768), with additional columns indicating lysosome (GO: 0005764)‐ or cholesterol‐related proteins.

sections.title: RNA Interference, Reverse Transcription, and Real‐Time PCR Analysis

paragraphs.en: Stealth siRNAs targeted to human TMEM55B (siTMEM55B#1, 5′‐ACGUGGAAGGCAAGAUGCAUCAGCA‐3′; siTMEM55B#2, 5′‐CAAGAUGCAUCAGCAUGUAGUCAAA‐3′), and nontargeting control were obtained from Invitrogen Life Technologies (Carlsbad, CA, USA). Human siRNAs were introduced into HeLa cells with the use of Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen Life Technologies) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The cells were then cultured for 48 h. Total RNA was isolated from cells with the use of an RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's protocol and was subjected to reverse transcription (RT) with the use of a QuantiTect Rev. Transcription Kit (Qiagen). The resulting cDNA was subjected to real‐time PCR analysis with Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix in an ABI‐Prism 7000 sequence detection system (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). The amounts of each target mRNA were calculated and normalized by that of GAPDH mRNA. Primers for PCR (forward and reverse, respectively) were as follows: 5′‐GTCAGTGGTGGACCTGACCTG‐3′ and 5′‐AAAGTGGTCGTTGAGGGCAAT‐3′ for human GAPDH; 5′‐CGAGTCTGCCAATCTCTCATC‐3′ and 5′‐AGTGCGGTCTGTGAACTCTGT‐3′ for human TMEM55B.

LysoTracker Red DND‐99 (0.2 μM) or LysoSensor Green DND‐189 (0.2 μM) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were added to cells for 1 h at 37°C according to the manufacturer's protocol. HeLa cells expressing plasmid‐encoded fluorescent proteins for 24 h or metabolically labeled with fluorescent probes were observed with an LSM800 confocal microscope (Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany), and the images were processed for calculation of fluorescence intensity with ZEN imaging software (Zeiss) as well as Fiji (ImageJ, https://fiji.sc). For quantification of LysoTracker‐positive puncta, individual cells were manually delineated as regions of interest (ROIs). Images were converted to 8‐bit grayscale and segmented in Fiji using a fixed intensity threshold of 20–255. Touching puncta were separated using an intensity‐maxima watershed algorithm with a prominence value of 20. The resulting objects were analyzed using the Analyze Particles function with a minimum particle area of 0.25 μm2 and a circularity range of 0.00–1.00. The number of LysoTracker‐positive puncta per cell and the area, aspect ratio, and fluorescence intensity of individual puncta were measured. For aspect ratio analysis, single LysoTracker‐positive puncta were selected using the following criteria to accurately assess lysosomal morphology: particle area, 0.25–1.00 μm2; minimum solidity, 0.925; peak prominence, 10; and maximum number of intensity peaks per particle, 1. Aspect ratio, defined as the ratio of the major to minor axis of the fitted ellipse, was measured using Fiji. LysoSensor‐positive puncta were quantified using the same procedure, except that a fixed intensity threshold of 40–255 and a minimum particle area of 0.10 μm2 were used. Puncta counts were determined for each cell, whereas the fluorescence intensity, area, and aspect ratio measurements obtained from individual puncta were summarized as the median for each cell.

Cell media of HeLa cells expressing organelle‐targeted Ca2+ indicators were pre‐incubated with HEPES‐buffered saline (HBS; 137 mM NaCl, 5.9 mM KCl, 2.2 mM CaCl2, 1.2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM HEPES, 14 mM glucose, pH 7.4) for 1 h at 37°C and then stimulated with ATP (200 μM) (Wako, Japan). The images were captured by the Operetta high‐content screening system (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA) using a ×20 objective (λ_ex 460–490 nm; λ_em 500–550 nm) at the time point of ATP addition (t = 0 s) and continued time points (t = X s) at a rate of one frame per 20 s for a total of 1240 s (G‐CEPIA) or 180 s (Ly‐GG and CEPIA3mt). The concentration of Ca2+ for each time point was calculated by ΔF/F0 = (Fx − F0)/F0. Images were analyzed by Harmony software (PerkinElmer).

HeLa cells were lysed in Triton lysis buffer containing 40 mM HEPES‐NaOH (pH 7.6), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% Triton X‐100, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM Na₃VO₄, 25 mM NaF, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM PMSF, leupeptin (10 μg/mL), and 10% glycerol. After 10 min on ice, lysates were centrifuged at 15000 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and protein concentrations were determined with the Pierce BCA Protein Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Extracts were resolved by SDS–PAGE, transferred to Immobilon‐P membranes (Merck Millipore, Darmstadt, Germany), and probed with primary antibodies. Signals were developed with SuperSignal reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and imaged on an LAS‐4000 (GE Healthcare, Waukesha, WI, USA).

Protein extracts were subjected to immunoprecipitation for 1 h at 4°C with primary antibodies and protein G–Sepharose 4 Fast Flow (Amersham Biosciences, Uppsala, Sweden). The immunoprecipitates were washed three times with cell lysis buffer and then subjected to immunoblot analysis.

Statistical analyses were performed using BellCurve for Excel (Social Survey Research Information Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). Normality within each group was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. For normally distributed data, two prespecified comparisons were analyzed using two‐sided Welch's t‐tests. In the knockdown experiments, siControl was compared with siTMEM55B#1 and siTMEM55B#2. In the rescue experiments, the control group was compared with the TMEM55B‐knockdown group, and the TMEM55B‐knockdown group was compared with the mouse TMEM55B rescue group. The two resulting p values within each experiment were adjusted as a single family using Holm's method.

For data that were not normally distributed, differences among the three groups were analyzed using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Steel's multiple‐comparison test for the same prespecified comparisons.

For imaging analyses, cells, rather than individual puncta, were used as the unit of analysis. The number of LysoTracker‐positive puncta was determined for each cell. Fluorescence intensity measurements from individual LysoTracker‐ and LysoSensor‐positive puncta, as well as area and aspect ratio measurements from individual LysoTracker‐positive puncta, were summarized as the median for each cell.

Data are presented as violin plots of individual cell‐level values or as the mean ± SEM, as indicated in the figure legends. Exact sample sizes, statistical tests, effect estimates expressed as mean differences (MDs) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) are provided in the corresponding figure legends. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 and is indicated as follows: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001; n.s., p ≥ 0.05.

figures.caption: Identification of PDZD8‐associated proteins by proteomic analysis. (A) Endosome‐related proteins identified as PDZD8‐associated proteins. Protein abundance was estimated semiquantitatively based on identification frequency (IF). Asterisks indicate proteins previously reported to be associated with TMEM55B. Lysosome (Ly)‐localized and cholesterol (Chol)‐related proteins are indicated. Proteins were classified according to Gene Ontology (GO) terms and UniProtKB annotations. (B, C) HeLa cells were transfected with (+) or without (−) PDZD8‐FLAG (B) or FLAG‐Protrudin (C) together with HA‐TMEM55B. Cell lysates were subjected to immunoprecipitation‐immunoblot (IP‐IB) analysis using anti‐FLAG, anti‐HA, and anti‐HSP90 antibodies. Input (0.3%) and FLAG‐immunoprecipitated fractions were analyzed. Anti‐HA immunoblots were additionally visualized using high‐sensitivity detection reagents. (D) HeLa cells were transfected with PDZD8‐FLAG (left), Myc‐Protrudin (middle), or HA‐TMEM55B (right). Cells were fixed and immunostained with antibodies to FLAG, Myc, and HA, respectively. (E, F, G) HeLa cells were transfected with HA‐TMEM55B and PDZD8‐FLAG (E), PDZD8‐FLAG and Myc‐Protrudin (F), or HA‐TMEM55B and Myc‐Protrudin (G). Cells were fixed and immunostained with antibodies to each tag.
